old_title: Manchester United confirm Pochettino appointment; Carrick thanks fans for 'love and support': football - live
new_title: Tearful Pochettino says leaving USA for Manchester United 'most difficult decision' of career: football - as it happened
old_text:
Mauricio Pochettino's switch from the US men's national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.
The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades.
Mauricio Pochettino is giving a surprisingly emotional press conference as he officially announces his departure from the USMNT for Manchester United following their next two games. When thanking officials for the opportunity he was given, his voice cracks and out comes a tissue to wipe away the tears.
An interesting take from Suzanne Wrack as Chelsea host Manchester City in the WSL on Saturday lunchtime. We'll have a live MBM blog on that one by the way.
We're all aware now that Pochettino's first game in charge is at Anfield. But what comes after that? His first six matches comprise four in the Premier League and two in the Champions League.
22 Nov: Liverpool v Man Utd 25 Nov: Sporting v Man Utd 28 Nov:Man Utd v Brentford
2 Dec: Newcastle v Man Utd 5 Dec:Man Utd v Coventry
8 Dec:Man Utd v RB Leipzig
Three away games in the first four isn't ideal or perhaps it is. Poch can start to bed in on the road where the away fans will perhaps give him more leeway. Sporting away is tough given that the Portuguese side have won three of their first four Champions League matches in the group phase. But Leipzig are down in 29th while Coventry and Newcastle are in the bottom half of the Premier League. Brentford sit 12th in the six-match EPL form table after two wins, two draws and two defeats. In other words, there are opportunities to turn the ship around.
Valérien Ismaël has been appointed as Le Havre coach until the end of the season, with the club sitting rock bottom in the Ligue 1 standings.
The 51-year-old former defender, who was hired as a replacement for Didier Digard, will face a huge task to keep Le Havre in the French top tier. Still winless in Ligue 1, Le Havre have two points from 10 matches.
The much-traveled Ismaël has coached teams in Germany, Greece, Austria, Turkey and England, and was most recently at Blackburn. Le Havre said in a statement yesterday that he has handled "emergency situations" in the past, "which could prove very useful in the coming weeks." AP
Will Carlos Baleba become a key man for United under Pochettino? Much has been made of the Argentinian's desire to see his teams run, run, and then run some more. In the space of one season at Chelsea, Pochettino improved their running stats.
Baleba looks to be the only current United midfielder with the legs to cover large spaces. Pochettino often prefers a 4-2-3-1, so surely it stands to reason that the former Brighton player will fit in as one of two deep-lying midfielders? Kobbie Mainoo would appear to be the ideal partner for Baleba - and we know Pochettino likes to promote young homegrown talent. What that means for summer signings Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, it remains to be seen. But the news that Bruno Fernandes probably won't sign a new contract, could mean a shift in the structure of United's midfield.
Santos was loaned out by Chelsea to Nottingham Forest and Strasbourg during Pochettino's sole campaign at Stamford Bridge. United may well look to recruit more hard-running midfielders in January or the summer to suit Pochettino's preferences.
Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu will step down next week, the country's football association revealed today, cutting short his tenure in the wake of the 2027 Asian Cup's postponement.
Moriyasu, Japan's longest-serving coach, was originally set to lead the team at the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January before handing the reins to current Under-23 boss Go Oiwa.
But the Asian Football Confederation announced last week that the tournament would be pushed back to December 2027 due to "exceptional circumstances" in the region, following Houthi attacks on the host country.
That left Moriyasu in limbo, with Japan Football Association (JFA) chiefs last week declining to clarify when the coaching handover would take place.
They said that Japan's friendlies in Singapore against Brazil on Saturday and Paraguay on Tuesday would be Moriyasu's last games in charge. AFP
Reports are already emerging suggesting Pochettino will bring Jesús Pérez, Miguel D'Agostino, Toni Jiménez, Sebastiano Pochettino (his son) and Sílvia Tuyà with him to Manchester United. Coaching squad, assemble!
Wow, that's quite the emotional and heartfelt message from Carrick, speaking directly to the United supporters. That's a bond that will not be broken, despite the events of the past few months.
He may not have been up to the job, but Carrick remained classy and dignified until the end.
Michael Carrick statement on Manchester United exit
The former head coach has taken to Instagram to address United fans and his departure from the club.
Dear United fans, I've had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love. There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I am incredibly grateful.
With that comes huge responsibility, and to be at Manchester United you need to understand exactly what that means. It's different to anywhere else.
Ultimately you need to push to be the best, but there is a culture, there are values and there are behaviours that you have to live by and respect, which have been built over a long period of time ...
I want to say a big thank you to the supporters. I must say, you are a special rare breed ...
I just wanted to give you something back. That love never dies. I know we've not had the results lately, but you've shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing ... would be to turn the other way. That means more than a win or two ...
I want nothing but success for Manchester United. This club has been such a big part of my life and that will never change. I'll always be proud to have played my part and I'll always want the very best for it.
I'll be right there with you from now on, watching from the sidelines, cheering the lads on.
Before I pivot away to other topics (yes, there is a big footballing world outside of Manchester United), there's still time to plug the latest Football Weekly, as the guys get to grips with Pochettino's appointment, among other things.
Robyn Cowen is joined by Jacob Steinberg, Lars Sivertsen and Paul Watson for this one.
It's been said a few times this week, but it's very modern day Manchester United to appoint an international manager during the international break ... the only time he's actually busy and has games to manage.
Pochettino's first day of work at Carrington will be on Wednesday, if he's recovered from the jet lag in time.
There's a general consensus in the emails below - and among most Manchester United fans right now - that the owners above Pochettino have made things even trickier for the incoming boss at Old Trafford.
Reader Jeff Sax, however, lies the blame in a slightly different direction. This is what he says on email:
People should stop blaming the owners. Management and players are responsible... if the management were not so bad maybe there would be better players.
And the players are not being professional in the way they are playing. Nothing to do with ownership.
Emails! Lots of emails! Lots of emails about Mauricio Pochettino and Manchester United ...
Darren Winter: "We all know that Pochettino is wedded to a basic 4-2-3-1, as were Carrick and Ten Hag, and the current United squad is apparently set up to play that way. But we also know that formations and tactics are cyclical. You would think that the next big team who changes the formation and nullifies 4-2-3-1 with something new will be the team leading the charge (cough Brighton cough), with others working out how to stop or adapt to the new formation.
"That got me thinking about Ruben Amorim. I wonder if that's what United thought they were doing with hiring a 3-4-2-1 manager? But the problem with that theory is that it gives Ineos a lot of credit for football knowledge they don't appear to have. So I don't know, what do you think?"
Paul Simpson: "It seems like the best in class hierarchy at Manchester United are up to their old tricks. A new manager was needed in the summer and as a fan i can fully understand the pull of appointing Carrick after the job he did last season. But Pochettino was coming out of contract after the World Cup so why was he not considered then? I guess it was so they could wait and pay the £10m or so compensation once he had signed a new contract plus whatever they need to pay Carrick for sacking him. It's decisions like these that show why Ratcliffe pays Wilcox and Berrada the big bucks."
Pochettino's confirmation as Manchester United's new head coach ends a run of near-misses that date back a decade.
He was linked with the post as far back as 2016, also coming close to being appointed in 2018, 2021 and 2022. He has long had an admirer in Sir Alex Ferguson, who praised Pochettino in a 2016 interview when the Argentinian's Spurs team were approaching their apex.
"This lad has composure," said Ferguson.
"You never see him ruffled and the way his team play is a testimony to the work he is doing.
"The most important thing for English football is how many English and young players are in his team. He understands the advantage of playing young people. They won't let you down and they have been fantastic."
United's own statement describes Pochettino as the club's new 'head coach' and reveals he will begin work on 18 November, with "Mauricio and his staff to be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the U.S. Men's National Team".
Pochettino's long-time assistants are Jesus Perez and Miguel D'Agostino, as well as goalkeeping coach Antonio Jimenez.
Here's Pochettino's statement on his departure from the USMNT:
The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country.
We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it's one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.
Mauricio Pochettino's switch from the US men's national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.
The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades.
It's going to be fascinating whether Pochettino is labelled a 'head coach' or a 'manager' when United confirm his appointment. We will soon see I suppose.
Here's another email from Krishna, who I think messaged my colleague David earlier on. It's a list of problems for Pochettino:
Hello Dominic. An unwilling captain, [a] chaotic board, non-existent management team, insufficient and disorganised recruiting, a completely frustrated fanbase and an owner who does not just care ...
Clearly the United job still has some allure, Krishna. Pochettino has coveted it for a long, long time.
There was a bit of a shock in the Nations League last night: Italy beat France 3-1 after going 1-0 down early on.
Are the Azzurri on their way back under Roberto Mancini? It's probably too soon to tell, but this was a positive, as France suffered their first defeat under Zinedine Zidane.
Let's pivot to other matters for a short while ... Andy Robertson will equal Scotland's men's appearance record if and when he takes the field against North Macedonia tonight. And although the legendary left-back is matching Kenny Dalglish's Scotland cap record, he insists he's a way off King Kenny in terms of footballing legacy and reputation.
Scotland also badly need a win to take the pressure off Sébastien Pocognoli, who isn't having things easy in charge of the Tartan Army. He's still looking for his first home win as Scotland head coach, this his third attempt.
Pochettino was viewed as having a very distinct philosophy at Tottenham: pressing, fast attacks, narrow wingers etc. These quotes show perhaps he is willing to go away from that, depending on the players at his disposal:
I need to adapt to my roster, my squad, and not to think about myself. [My job is] not to coach the squad for myself. I need to coach the team for the team, for the players, not for what I think is good for me. I need to provide the best tools to perform with the characteristics that I have in my squad.
I think much of the chatter around Pochettino, rightly or wrongly, still centres on his (excellent) Tottenham tenure. This interview from earlier this year gives more of an insight into the modern day Poch, how he's changed and adapted from those years at Spurs.
The PSG-Chelsea-USA run perhaps isn't the most convincing, but there is important context around all those jobs.
Time to test the grey matter as you down a cuppa - and WFHers ponder whether to put the heating on. Plenty of football in this week's quiz. While you mull which Manchester United boss has spent the longest in the job since Fergie left, I'll hand the reins to Dominic Booth.
After several decades of hurt, the world's favourite sport may finally be getting its artistic due, writes Emma John. In related news, I was in Afflecks Palace in Manchester on Wednesday, admiring some of Stan Chow's football pop art. Plenty of Christmas present potential there although I'll also point you to The Guardian Bookshop.
Kane's lead at the top of the England all-time top scorers chart is ridiculous! Just eight more before he brings up the century. For so long, trying to beat Sir Bobby Charlton's tally of 49 seemed a massive ask. Fair play to the presumably very fashion-conscious Vivian Woodward for that goals per game ratio.
Barney Ronay was at Wembley on Thursday night to celebrate Happy Harry Kane day.
"And as the teams lined up there was a surprise appearance from the real star of this stage, the Ballon d'Or itself, wreathed in event glamour and star-flash. Kane drew the ballon from its stone in Arthurian fashion, then held it a little sheepishly in one hand. Prince William walked out and gave him a massive framed shirt, which seemed weird in the moment, like the chief area sales manager presenting the prize from the Christmas raffle. Has Prince William ever been asked to carry anything before?"
Here's David Hytner's report of England's 2-1 win over Croatia in the Nations League last night. Comes complete with photo of Harry Kane in classic penalty-taking pose.
Arsenal are struggling domestically but they dug out a fine result away to Barcelona in the Women's Champions League last night. The result left Renée Slegers' side fourth in the table. Remember, the top four in the 18-team group phase qualify automatically for the quarter-finals. Here's Suzanne Wrack's report.
Fernandes rejects second offer of new United contract
Will Unwin
The Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second offer of a new contract at Old Trafford but the club are confident of getting the midfielder to commit his future to Old Trafford. The 32-year-old's current deal runs until the end of the season but United have the option to trigger a further year.
If United elect not to utilise that clause, Fernandes would be allowed to speak to clubs abroad in January. The Portuguese has previously had interest from Saudi Arabia and Galatasaray but chose to stay.
Fernandes won the PFA player of the year award last season after helping United to third in the league with a record-breaking 21 assists, but his form has dipped. He also took aim at Carrick's tactics after United's defeat by Como in the Champions League, in the weeks before the manager was sacked.
Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be appointed as the new Manchester United head coach later today. The Argentinian will leave his role with the United States to sign a two-and-a-half year contract at Old Trafford as Michael Carrick's replacement.
Carrick and his backroom staff were dismissed on Thursday, with Pochettino expected to bring his trusted lieutenants from previous roles with him.
It will cost United £7m in compensation to secure the former Tottenham and Chelsea boss.
A Poch timeline for you. The official announcement is expected later today but Pochettino won't arrive at the club until next Wednesday. Here's how the next 10 days look:
Friday 13 November: United are set to confirm his appointment.
Saturday 14 November: He takes charge of the USA in the first leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti in Miami (9.30pm UK time).
Tuesday 17 November: He leads the USA for the last time, in the second leg against Haiti in Cincinnati (midnight UK time).
Wednesday 18 November: He flies to Manchester to meet his new bosses.
Thursday 19 November: He takes his first training session with the players.
Sunday 22 November: His first game in charge is Liverpool away at Anfield (4.30pm). Gulp!
Ahead of Mauricio Pochettino's unveiling at Manchester United, Andrew Beasley crunches the numbers to look at the Argentine's possible impact.
An elite manager? The stats say yes: only the five "big beasts" of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Pochettino.
Jack Grealish has issued a public apology to Everton fans after he made his comeback in a behind-closed-doors match with Derby. Grealish has missed four matches and not played for the Toffees since 17 October following a breach of club discipline.
Boss David Moyes has been reluctant to discuss any finer details and the club only confirmed the 31-year-old former England winger was "not match-fit" ahead of a trip to Newcastle on 2 November but Grealish featured in a friendly at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday in the strongest suggestion yet that a line has been drawn over the issue.
"Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training," Grealish wrote on his Instagram story.
"I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks. I love playing for this club and can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt. See you all soon."
Grealish spent the first half of the 2025-26 campaign on loan at Everton before injury curtailed his spell on Merseyside, but he returned on another temporary deal on transfer deadline day. (Press Association)
Good morning! Harry Kane scores for England and more managerial chaos at Manchester United. Yep, some things never change.
Kane's penalty, on his record 126th appearance for the Three Lions, secured England's 2-1 victory over Croatia in the Nations League on Thursday night. Earlier in the day, Michael Carrick had been sacked by Manchester United, paving the way for Mauricio Pochettino to take over the reins at Old Trafford.
We'll have reaction to those big events, women's Champions League and Nations League updates plus news of an apology from Jack Grealish to Everton. In other words, lots to talk about and dissect!
new_text:
Mauricio Pochettino's switch from the US men's national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.
The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades.
Right, that's all we have time for. There is, however, a new blog to follow, with Scott Murray helming our coverage of Scotland's Nations League clash with North Macedonia. Goodnight.
Richard Hirst has something to add. "With Carrick, and presumably his assistants, gone and the new management, sorry coaches, not arriving till the middle of next week, is this the moment when the traffic cones have actually taken over training at Utd? You really couldn't make it up. Carry on SJR/Jason, you're doing a great job."
Joshua Keeling mails in with his thoughts on United's new ePoch (sorry). "Pochettino will probably fail, given the mess United are in. But I desperately hope he succeeds. He's a club builder, hopefully the club give him the tools he needs."
In other news, the Aberdeen chair, Dave Cormack, has admitted the club's financial performance "falls short of the standards we set ourselves" after their latest accounts showed an operating loss of £6.2m.
Aberdeen reported a record turnover of £24.4m for the year up to 30 June 2026, which the club attributed to participation in the Conference League last season alongside "strong performances across commercial, retail, ticketing and hospitality operations".
But they posted an Ebitda (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) loss of £4m and an operating loss of £6.2m, compared with a loss of £1.5m in the previous financial year.
The club finished ninth in the Scottish Premiership last term after sacking their manager, Jimmy Thelin, in January and put their financial losses down to increased investment in football operations, a "disappointing" season on the pitch, increased operating costs and lower gains from player sales.
"While we are pleased to report record turnover, the overall financial outcome falls short of the standards we set ourselves and reflects the significant challenges experienced during the 2025-26 season," Cormack said. "The board made a conscious decision to invest heavily in the football department with the aim of driving success on the pitch. Unfortunately, the performances and results achieved did not deliver the return we expected from that investment, and that is reflected in these results.
"That said, the underlying strength of the club's revenue streams continues to be encouraging. Achieving record turnover and record partnership revenue demonstrates the continued loyalty of our supporters, the commitment of our commercial partners, and the hard work of our staff across all areas of the business." Press Association
Any sleepless Socceroos fans following along? Australia have beaten Qatar 3-0 in their friendly in Doha, Riley McGree, Tete Yengi and Nestory Irankunda nabbing the goals. Here's a full report.
Well, hello there. As the blog heads into injury time, we've got an email from Peter Oh. "I'm trying really hard not to have a major tissue, I mean issue with Poch's tears," he writes. "But let's be honest. It's all a bit performative, isn't it?"
Tonight's schedule is mainly Nations League stuff.
Netherlands v Greece, Serbia v Germany, Scotland v North Macedonia and Slovenia v Switzerland are all 7.45pm (GMT) kick-offs in Leagues A and B, while Moldova are 1-0 up versus Kazakhstan at half-time of their League C game.
That's all from me. Will Magee will guide you through till closing time.
Pep Guardiola to become Pochettino's successor at the USMNT? That's what the swirling rumours are already suggesting at this very early stage. We shall see ...
Nations League: Konrad Laimer is convinced Austria can beat the Republic of Ireland in Linz in their Saturday night clash despite the absence of key personnel.
Austria are in control of their own destiny, leading the group by three points heading into their final two fixtures, and would earn automatic promotion to League A with victory over the Republic.
Ralf Rangnick has been dealt a double blow, adding Xaver Schlager and Alexander Prass to an ever-growing list of injured players ahead of the Ireland match and Tuesday's group-stage closer against Israel.
"We have to exert some pressure," said Laimer. "We have to look to see if we can get some chances to score goals. The Republic of Ireland have a good team, but I think if we perform well we can win the game tomorrow." PA
Transfer rumour: It has not taken long for Manchester United to be linked with a Pochettino-coded player. Reports suggest United are taking an interest in Como and Argentina attacker Nico Paz, who terrorised Michael Carrick's side in their recent 4-1 Champions League defeat in Italy.
Paz is the son of former Argentina international Pablo Paz, an old teammate of Pochettino's with Newell's Old Boys.
I received this email during my earlier stint on the blog about the new head coach, via reader Ronnie. I've not seen a whole heap of anti-Poch stuff today - the bile/anger has mainly been directed at those above him at United - but it's an interesting argument.
United need a big personality and, to be frank, the meanness in Deschamps or Tuchel. Very surprised at the Poch appointment. He seems a good guy, perhaps too nice, with a positive playing style and the players, in good times, loved him.
But in bad times it's been a disaster. PSG? Couldn't deal with the big characters. Spurs? Falling to pieces when they should have been kicking on after losing the Champions League final. Shipping 7 against Munich at home in 2019? The players wanted him gone.
Yes he has a temper to scold but, in the end, he's too soft and cannot deal with strong or turbulent characters. It's simply not a quality in his bag and that's not going to change. The players will walk all over him like a doormat.
Meanwhile, the execs won't leave him and the dressing room alone to do the job. And poor Poch simply has not got the wherewithal in those narrow shoulders to deal with the bullies, the melodrama, nor the size of United.
Simon was too modest to plug it too much, but I enjoyed his illuminating passage in the latest Football Daily newsletter (are you subscribed yet?) on Pierre Sage's ill-fated stint as Crystal Palace manager:
His supporters, such as they are, would argue he was hobbled by knack, suspensions and poor transfer dealings, and approximately nothing went to plan for the man who just six months ago was revelling in being named Ligue 1 coach of the year. His philosophy just never quite translated. "There are two types of teams: one with the ball, and the other chasing it," he said last year. "I prefer to be the first of those." And it is true that in Ligue 1 last season only Paris St-Germain and Marseille had, on average, more of the ball than his Lens side. But it turned out that Crystal Palace players were quite happy chasing it thank you, whichever of them he picked - and he picked most of them, fielding more players than any other club this season.
Very kind of you Simon. Maybe Pochettino's tears were simply a result of thinking about the huge undertaking he's about to tackle at Old Trafford?
It seems to be he's starting from the very very bottom, with no guarantee that things will automatically improve. More Poch/United stuff in the next hour? You bet!
Here's the definitive update from Pablo Iglesias Maurier at Mauricio Pochettino's press conference in Fayetteville, Georgia.
There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino's news conference at US Soccer's national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks - they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.
"I think [the decision was]," Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, "one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much."
The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.
Laura Cochrane has written about Jude Bellingham's commercial savvy. Warning: this article contains photos of Bellingham's naked torso. As one public relations consultant tells her:
Bellingham is an exceptional sporting talent, and his brand value is understandably enormous. But fashion doesn't create that value, football does. Fashion merely provides another means of exploiting it.
Pablo Maurer, who covers USMNT for us, was at training today to see Mauricio Pochettino saying a few (almost) farewells, including this embrace with Christian Pulisic. The two are not believed to have a close relationship, though last year Pulisic said this:
We have good conversations. Honestly. Probably what you guys experience and what the media sees is a bit not exactly what we experience. Things are good. We spoke. We had a normal camp and everything is good between us, good between the team. There's probably not as much drama as you guys think there is.
Don't worry, human rights, Uefa's got your back. Here's Reuters:
Uefa has established a Human Rights Advisory Board to provide independent oversight and advice during the planning and delivery of Euro 2028, the governing body said on Friday.
The board will serve as a platform for constructive dialogue, external scrutiny and specialist guidance on identifying, preventing and mitigating human rights risks linked to the tournament.
The initiative builds on Uefa's previous work with Human Rights Advisory Boards established for Euro 2024 in Germany and Women's Euro 2025 in Switzerland.
"The Human Rights Advisory Board brings valuable independent perspectives and constructive challenge, helping us stay proactive as preparations progress and ensuring our commitments translate into meaningful action," Uefa's vice-president and board chair Laura McAllister said.
Euro 2028 will be jointly hosted by England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
We've been sent some photos of England's players hard at work at Tottenham's training ground today. I liked them, so here they are. Or some of them, anyway:
Hello everyone! I begin my time at the helm with some reaction to, yes, Pochettino's appointment by Manchester United. Here are the thoughts of Henry James "Harry" Redknapp:
Someone said to me today, 'What a bad time to take the job', I said, 'I could never think of a better time to take over the Man United job'. They are rock-bottom. There's only one way, it's up. It isn't like David Moyes following Alex Ferguson. David Moyes is a great manager, but following Fergie was impossible. Now he [Pochettino] takes over a club that is in a real mess at the moment, and he can only take one take them one way, and that is going to be up. I like him. He's a great character, very clever manager, knows the game, and I'm sure he'll do a good job. But it's going to be two or three years before you see Man United anywhere near what you'd hope they would be.
And here are the thoughts of Harry's son, Jamie Redknapp:
He's an elite manager. I'm sure that [sporting director] Jason Wilcox, [chief executive] Omar Barada are probably thinking to themselves, 'Are we lucky to keep our jobs?'. I think the answer to that would be yes, if they are to stay with that structure and regime. He's coming into an environment now that's going to be so difficult, he's probably going to think after a few months, 'Wow, have I made the right decision here?'. One of the biggest clubs in the world, but for the last few years has been so poorly run.
I regret to report that the thoughts of Jamie's children Charley, Beau and Raphael are currently unknown.
Pochettino is doing his best not to talk about Manchester United - yet. But he does finally give away something.
I think we will have time next week to talk about Manchester United, but now I think it is much better to talk about us, about USA Soccer, and of course, USA Men National Team, and we have two games ahead, and now it is focus complete on this.
However, when pressed about why he's leaving after just signing a new deal with the USMNT, he does throw us a little nugget.
There's not too many opportunities that happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives it is difficult to turn down.
Pochettino is asked if he's satisfied about what he achieved during his time at USMNT.
I think it's difficult in that business, always you want more, and then you are a critic, and you say, 'oh, I could be better, I should do better things, do better things'.
Always it's being brave, take the best decision, to get the experience from that decision, what happened, and try to adapt again, and to try to make better decisions for the future.
I don't like to use satisfaction, being satisfied of what happened in the past. That's always, I think, in our mindset, it's always we try to do better, and do better and try to find a way to, maybe in this similar situation, act in the always best way.
Pochettino composes himself. Aware that this is U.S. Soccer goodbye rather than a Manchester United hello, his focus is on his time in charge of USMNT. He dodges the question on what appealed about the United job.
I want to thank the fans for the support, for everything. And of course, always, it was a tough moment.

Moriyasu, Japan's longest-serving coach, was originally set to lead the team at the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January before handing the reins to current Under-23 boss Go Oiwa.

Jack Grealish has issued a public apology to Everton fans after he made his comeback in a behind-closed-doors match with Derby. Grealish has missed four matches and not played for the Toffees since 17 October following a breach of club discipline. Boss David Moyes has been reluctant to discuss any finer details and the club only confirmed the 31-year-old former England winger was "not match-fit" ahead of a trip to Newcastle on 2 November but Grealish featured in a friendly at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday in the strongest suggestion yet that a line has been drawn over the issue. "Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training," Grealish wrote on his Instagram story. "I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks. I love playing for this club and can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt. See you all soon." Grealish spent the first half of the 2025-26 campaign on loan at Everton before injury curtailed his spell on Merseyside, but he returned on another temporary deal on transfer deadline day.
